## Move 1: physics behind a RESTful interface {#solver-interface data-section="2"}

![](figs/arch_moves.svg){fig-align="center" width="97%"}

::: {style="font-size:0.92em; margin-top:0.35em;"}
`checkpoint()` returns the solver's complete state as an opaque buffer;
`restore()` rebuilds it, and the transient continues as if it had never been
interrupted. [For RELAP5 this meant replacing the disk-based restart with an
in-memory one.]{style="color:#B40000;"}
:::

::: {.notes}
Move one. On the left is the engine as it was: the PRA core and RELAP5
compiled into one process. On the right is the same core, but every access to
the physics now goes through a solver interface, and the core asks for exactly
five things: advance time, apply an intervention, report state, checkpoint,
and restore.

There are two implementations. RELAP5 still runs in process, which keeps the
validated coupling. And a REST client drives any external solver over HTTP:
that is the RESTful interface.

The checkpoint is the key element. It returns the complete state as an opaque
buffer, and restore rebuilds it, so the transient continues as if never
interrupted. For RELAP5, that meant replacing the disk-based restart with an
in-memory one.
:::

## The whole interface: six endpoints {#rest-contract data-section="2"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
::: {style="font-size:0.94em;"}
| **Endpoint** | **Purpose** |
|:-------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| `POST /sessions` | create a solver session, fresh or from a restart |
| `POST /sessions/:id/advance` | integrate forward by *dt*; return the full state |
| `POST /sessions/:id/intervene` | apply operator actions as index and value pairs |
| `POST /sessions/:id/checkpoint` | snapshot the state; return a checkpoint id |
| `POST /sessions/:id/restore` | rewind the session to a checkpoint |
| `DELETE /sessions/:id` | destroy the session, free its resources |
:::
:::
::: {.column width="43%"}
```{=html}
<div class="facts">
  <div class="fact"><b>A solver is a service that holds sessions</b><span>each one an independent solver instance with its full state</span></div>
  <div class="fact"><b>Every advance returns five generic arrays</b><span>volumes, junctions, control variables, variable trips, logical trips</span></div>
  <div class="fact"><b>The mapper lives on the solver side</b><span>it packs native state into the arrays; the engine never parses a domain field</span></div>
  <div class="fact"><b>Trips fire once and latch</b><span>pivotal events come from trip firings, so branching semantics travel with the contract</span></div>
</div>
```
:::
::::

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.5em;"}
[Coupling a new code means implementing six endpoints: not merging code, not
matching a compiler, not sharing a process.]{style="color:#B40000;"}
:::

::: {.slideref}
Paths abbreviated; all routes live under `/api/v1`. Two read-only routes complete the contract: the current state without advancing time, and a liveness check.
:::

::: {.notes}
This table is the whole interface, which the paper calls the solver contract.
The solver is a service that holds sessions. Six endpoints change state, and
two only read.

The data format is deliberately generic. Every advance returns five arrays:
volumes, junctions, control variables, and two kinds of trips. A mapper on the
solver side packs the solver's own state into those arrays, so the engine
never parses a plant-specific field.

Trips fire once and latch, and the engine derives pivotal events from them, so
the rules for branching are part of the interface.

Coupling a new code means implementing these six endpoints: not merging code,
not matching a compiler, not sharing a process.
:::

## The interface in action {#anim-coupling data-section="2" background-iframe="assets/anim/coupling-animation.html" background-interactive="true" visibility="uncounted" .no-band}

::: {.notes}
[Animation, about thirty-eight seconds. It starts by itself and stops on its
last picture; the slide PDF shows that picture only.]

Here is the interface in action, as one sequence. On the left, the engine; in
the middle, the six verbs; on the right, an advanced reactor simulator in
RELAP5's place: for example SAM, SAS4A/SASSYS-1, RELAP5-3D, MELCOR, or your
own code. None of these is coupled yet; the point is that the engine does not
care which.

A trip fires inside an advance response and becomes a pivotal event. The
checkpoint comes back as a token that the engine never looks inside, and the
restore takes the other branch.

At the bottom right are the two services that use this interface today: a PWR
and a space reactor.
:::
